UAM noise routing · Austin, TX · session 3 · complete

When a Principle Binds

Sessions 1–2 found that the five fairness principles barely differed, and that what difference there was fell inside the solver’s own indifference. This session moved the study to an operating point where the principles actually constrain the routing — and the constraint does something the earlier regime could not show.

solver Z3 4.16.0, unmodified budget unlimited, harvest at H = 3600 s per cell K = 4 aircraft orderings setup D = 6, protected = {14, 4, 8} snapshot 2026-09-12 03:15, sweep complete
Sweep complete: 192 cells, 184 answered. All six conditions are proven in all four orderings at every fleet size from N = 6 to 24. Above that the ladder thins: cells that had not proved after one hour were stopped and their routings salvaged, and eight cells — Equal at N = 30 and 32 — produced no routing their own search could verify. Findings below rest on the proven range unless they say otherwise.

The question

Was the problem the principles, or the operating point?

The earlier sessions measured five principles at the workshop tool’s own default settings and found almost nothing separating them. That result had two possible readings: the principles genuinely do the same thing on this map, or the default settings give them nothing to do. Distinguishing those is what this session is for, and the answer turns out to be the second.

FINDING 01

At the tool’s default settings, two of the five principles return the no-fairness routing exactly — not approximately.

Running each condition under six different aircraft orderings at the default setup, Equal and Sufficientarian produce the same peak added noise, the same maximum aircraft per tile, the same total added noise and the same trip lengths as the baseline, ordering for ordering, at N = 8. At N = 16 and 24 they differ, but by less than one condition varies on its own when only the aircraft ordering changes.

Prioritarian’s objective evaluated to exactly zero everywhere, and the reason was not the principle. Its protected set — the three loudest non-vertiport tiles — carries zero aircraft-timesteps in the baseline routing at every fleet size. Nobody was ever going to fly there, so protecting it cost nothing.

FINDING 02

Making every principle active needs two changes, and neither works alone.

A screen of 100 cells — five candidate setups, four conditions plus a control, four orderings each, all proven — tested each principle against what that principle is: a cap is active if it binds, an objective is active if switching it off changes what it is supposed to protect.

Active principles at N = 16, by candidate setup. D6 caps every principle at 6 dB of added noise; protA moves the protected set onto the corridor, to the three busiest non-vertiport communities that are also low-income.
setupEqualSufficientarianPrioritarian UtilitarianProportionalactive
D6 / D5 yesyes no——2/5
protA nono yes——1/5
D6_protA / D5_protA yesyes yesyes yes5/5

With the protected set on the corridor, the ablation control puts 3.45 dB on the protected communities and the objective removes it entirely. The two decibel objectives beat the baseline’s score on their own metric by more than the indifference floor (17.9 against 16.1, and 504.5 against 16.1). D6 was chosen over D5 on attributable differences at N = 24 — 2 of 6 metrics against 1 — and because the looser cap is likelier to stay solvable at the top of the ladder.

FINDING 03

A binding cap does not merely lower the peak noise — it removes the arbitrariness in it.

This is the result that did not exist in the earlier regime, and it is the one worth taking to the paper.

Every cell here is solved four times under four aircraft orderings. The orderings leave the problem mathematically identical — same fleet, same origin–destination pairs, same feasible set — so the spread across them is pure tie-break: which of many equally-optimal routings the solver happened to return. For the un-capped baseline that spread reaches 3.98 dB of peak added noise. For every capped condition, from N = 14 upward, it is exactly zero.

Spread in peak added noise across four aircraft orderings (dB). Zero means all four orderings returned the same peak — the cap determines it. The baseline has no cap, and its peak is whatever the tie-break happens to produce.
conditionN=6N=8N=14N=16 N=22N=24
Baseline no cap 0.001.762.22 2.221.763.98
Equal0.001.76 0.000.000.00 0.00
Sufficientarian1.760.00 0.000.000.00 0.00
Prioritarian0.000.00 0.000.000.00 0.00

The capped conditions return a peak of 4.77 dB every single time from N = 14 on, while the baseline wanders between 5.64 and 7.70 dB depending on nothing anyone chose. Capacity utilisation sits at exactly 1.00, also with zero spread: the cap is binding on some community at some timestep, in all four orderings.

Why this matters beyond the instance: session 2 established that most differences between principles were smaller than the variation within one principle, and so could not be attributed to the principle. A binding constraint inverts that. It does not just move the outcome — it makes the outcome determinate, which is a property a community on the ground can actually rely on.

FINDING 04

The ladder carries five principles instead of two once the two objectives run in their count-weighted form — but the size of that gain is not yet measured cleanly.

Utilitarian and Proportional stall because both objectives are decibel-valued lookups: Z3 has to drive a table of dB expressions to its optimum and then prove it there. The solver already exposes a count-weighted form of each, described in the paper’s encoding section, selected by request parameters that cost no change to the solver at all. In count form both objectives prove every cell screened, four orderings out of four, at N = 6, 8 and 16.

Correction. An earlier version of this page put speedups of 51× and 1110× here. Those numbers compare the decibel form measured on the old setup (cap D = 10, protected set off the corridor) against the count form measured on the new one (D = 6, protected set on it). Two things differ, not one, so they attribute to the encoding an effect that also contains the cap change. They have been withdrawn. The comparison that would settle it — the decibel form on the new setup, same cap, same protected set — has not been run.
What is actually measured. The two rows on the left were solved on the old setup and the two on the right on the new one, so the columns are not a controlled comparison and no ratio is quoted between them.

What survives the objection is the qualitative gap at N = 16: the decibel form did not prove in 15.4 hours and the count form proves in 26 and 119 seconds. A difference of four orders of magnitude is not something a cap moving from 10 to 6 dB produces — on this ladder the cap-based conditions all solve within a factor of three of each other. So the ladder does carry five principles because of the encoding. But the magnitude is unquantified, and so is the question of whether the two encodings return the same routing, which was the other half of what this step was meant to establish.

Outstanding. Run the decibel form on the new setup at N = 6 and 8, four orderings, unlimited, and compare both the solve time and the returned routing against the count form under the attributability test. Proportional in decibel form took roughly eight hours per run at N = 8 on the old setup, so that sweep is an overnight job.

THE MAP

Every solve in the study, drawn: eight fleet sizes down, six conditions across.

Rows are fleet sizes, columns are conditions, and each panel draws the routing one ordering returned — every aircraft’s path, with line width proportional to the traffic on that leg. Circles are the two origins and the destination; the tile shading is the community’s ambient level, 45 to 65 dBA. The paper prints four of these rows; all eight are here.

Figure 2 (full). The central result is the N = 14 row and everything below it: five principles, five different objectives, and one identical peak — 4.77 dB — while the baseline in the last column climbs from 5.64 to 7.70. From that row on, the cap is binding, and a binding cap removes the arbitrariness: the peak stops depending on which optimal routing the solver happened to pick. The pictures still differ — the paths a principle chooses are its own — but the number they are chosen for does not. The bottom two rows were stopped at the one-hour horizon; their dense tangles are what an unfinished search looks like, not what the principle asks for.

THE METRICS

The same 46 cells as seven curves, and then as a table of every number behind them.

Each panel is one performance metric against fleet size. The shaded band around a line is that condition’s permutation band — the spread across four aircraft orderings of the identical problem. A band is the width of the solver’s own indifference, so two lines only differ if their means are further apart than the wider band and the bands do not overlap. Lines break at cells that were harvested rather than proven; those appear as isolated hollow markers, because a stopped search is not a sample from the optimal set and joining it to a curve draws a trend that was never solved for.

Peak added noise (top left) is the study in one panel: five principles pinned flat on 4.77 dB from N = 14 with no visible band at all, and a baseline that wanders above them inside a grey band up to four decibels wide — the same problem, the same optimum, four different answers. Congestion (max aircraft per tile, shared tile-timesteps) separates nothing: every principle sits inside the baseline’s band at every size. Travel time splits along the two families — average trip length is flat everywhere, so the caps pay in extra fleet hops from N = 22 while the objectives pay in departure delay instead. Total added noise is the one metric on which a principle beats the baseline outright: Proportional, along the bottom of that panel, lower at all six proven sizes with a zero band throughout, and attributably lower at five of them — N = 24 misses only because the baseline’s own band there is 25 dB wide.

Every cell of the ladder: means over four aircraft orderings, with the permutation band beside the mean where the orderings disagreed. A value in green has a band of exactly zero where some other condition at the same size did vary — all four orderings returned it, and the ordering was free to matter. Harvested cells were stopped at the one-hour horizon and carry a verified incumbent, not a proved optimum; their travel-time figures include the cost of having been stopped, so they bound the principle rather than stating it. Wall time is the mean seconds per solve, unlimited Z3 budget.

Reading the table. peak dB is the loudest single community’s added noise over the whole run; total dB sums added noise over every affected community and timestep. max/tile and shared t-steps are congestion — the most aircraft ever over one community, and the number of tile-timesteps holding more than one. avg hops is mean trip length, extra hops the fleet’s total distance above the no-fairness baseline at the same size, and dep. delay the aircraft-timesteps spent waiting to launch. The last two are the two currencies a principle can pay in, and which one it picks is the clearest signature in the table.

One principle at a time

Five head-to-head experiments

Everything above compares the principles with each other. The five sections below take them one at a time against the same control — the no-fairness baseline at the same fleet size, the same demand, the same orderings — and ask three questions of each. Did it achieve the thing it was asked to achieve, scored on its own objective? What did it cost in added noise, in congestion, and in travel time? And does any of that clear the solver’s indifference?

Scoring the objective on both routings is what makes the first question answerable. The solver only reports the objective a run was optimising, so the baseline — which optimises nothing — carries no score for any of them. The three objectives are therefore recomputed from the stored routings by harness/objectives.py, which checks itself against the values the solver did report: all 32 runs for each of the three, reproduced exactly.

EXPERIMENT 01 · EQUAL vs BASELINE

A cap on any one community’s level. Nothing separates it from the baseline until the cap binds, and then it buys 1.93 dB off the peak for 2.75 extra fleet-hops.

Equal (top) over the no-fairness baseline (bottom), the same problem at each fleet size with and without the principle. Panel titles carry peak added noise and fleet hops above the shortest-path floor; a dagger marks a cell stopped at the one-hour horizon.

What the principle was asked to do

Equal is not an objective at all — it is a hard cap, so there is no score to minimise and the question is only whether the cap binds. Utilisation is the busiest tile’s occupancy as a fraction of what D = 6 allows it: 2 aircraft over a 45 dBA community, 29 over a 55, 298 over a 65. At 1.00 the cap is the thing deciding the routing; the baseline runs at 0.00 because its cap is wide enough never to be reached.

Capacity utilisation of the busiest tile: 1.00 means the cap is holding the routing against its limit, and is marked. Below 1.00 nothing in the routing is touching the cap, so the principle is not the thing choosing it.

The cap goes from slack to binding between N = 8 and N = 14, and everything this principle does to the routing happens after that. Below it the cap is a constraint the routing was never going to violate, and Equal and the baseline are the same condition wearing different labels.

EXPERIMENT 03 · PRIORITARIAN vs BASELINE

Weights the worst-off communities first, and empties them completely: its objective is zero at every fleet size, in every ordering. It is also the only cap that lowers total added noise attributably before its cap binds, and later it buys the same quieter peak for the least distance of the three.

Prioritarian (top) over the no-fairness baseline (bottom), the same problem at each fleet size with and without the principle. Panel titles carry peak added noise and fleet hops above the shortest-path floor; a dagger marks a cell stopped at the one-hour horizon. The three protected communities are outlined: the baseline flies straight through them, and the principle does not.

What the principle was asked to do

Prioritarian minimises the added noise summed over the three protected communities across every timestep — stations 4, 8 and 14, outlined on the maps above. The baseline optimises nothing and is scored here on the same quantity, so the two columns are the same objective evaluated on two routings.

Prioritarian’s own objective (dB summed over stations 4, 8, 14), lower is better, evaluated on both routings. Bands are over the four orderings. The last column is the same indifference test the rest of the page uses. Attributably better than the baseline at N = 16, 22.

The objective is driven to exactly zero at every fleet size, in all four orderings. Not low — zero: no aircraft is ever over a protected community, at any timestep, at any size on the ladder. The baseline puts 2.2 to 11.0 dB on the same three communities and swings by up to 16.8 depending on nothing but aircraft ordering. Two of the six sizes clear the indifference floor; the other four miss only because the baseline’s own band is wider than the gap, which is a statement about how arbitrary the baseline is, not about what the principle achieved. This is the cleanest result in the study, and it is invisible in every aggregate metric — the protected set is three tiles, and what happens on them washes out of a map-wide total.

EXPERIMENT 04 · UTILITARIAN vs BASELINE

Minimises fleet transit time — and the baseline already minimises it, exactly, at every size. The objective is inert, so what this condition returns is a tie-break; it still buys a quieter peak, and pays for it in departure delay rather than distance.

Utilitarian (top) over the no-fairness baseline (bottom), the same problem at each fleet size with and without the principle. Panel titles carry peak added noise and fleet hops above the shortest-path floor; a dagger marks a cell stopped at the one-hour horizon.

What the principle was asked to do

Utilitarian in count form minimises total fleet transit time: the aircraft-timesteps between an aircraft’s first move and its arrival, summed over the fleet. The baseline is scored on the same quantity.

Utilitarian’s own objective (fleet transit, aircraft-timesteps), lower is better, evaluated on both routings. Bands are over the four orderings. The last column is the same indifference test the rest of the page uses. No size on the ladder separates the two on this objective.

The objective is inert. Fleet transit time is identical to the baseline’s at all eight sizes on the ladder, to the aircraft-timestep, and at the seven where both sides are proven the band on each is zero — the quantity Utilitarian minimises is already at its floor before the objective is switched on, because every aircraft is already flying a shortest path. So Utilitarian’s distinctive routings are tie-breaks among equally optimal answers, not the result of optimisation, and that is also why it is the cheapest condition in the study to solve: the objective prunes the search without ever having to trade anything away. The departure delay it does pay is real, but it is not bought by this objective — transit time is measured from first move to arrival and does not count waiting on the ground.

EXPERIMENT 05 · PROPORTIONAL vs BASELINE

Burden follows benefit, by proximity ring. It is the only condition that beats the baseline on total added noise at every proven size, and it does it by concentrating traffic rather than spreading it.

FINDING 05

In the new regime the caps cost travel time and buy quieter peaks — attributably, from N = 22.

Across the whole of sessions 1–2, no principle ever flew further than the shortest-path floor except in a one-decibel window at the very edge of feasibility. At D = 6 that changes: from N = 22 all three cap-based conditions fly further than the no-fairness baseline and land a quieter peak, and both differences clear the indifference floor.

Difference from the no-fairness baseline at the same fleet size, where the difference exceeds the permutation band at that cell. Congestion never clears the floor; the bands on maximum aircraft per tile stay wide (4 to 6 aircraft).
conditionextra hops vs baseline peak added noiseattributable from
Equal+3−1.93 dBN = 22
Sufficientarian+3−1.93 dBN = 22
Prioritarian+2−1.93 dBN = 22

So the trade a fairness cap makes on this map is now visible and measurable: two to three fleet-hops of extra flying, for about two decibels off the worst-affected community’s peak, and for an outcome that no longer depends on which optimal routing the solver picked.

FINDING 06

Above N = 25 the two caps stop behaving alike, and one of them stops being solvable.

Above 25 aircraft the tool stops sending an absolute cap to Equal and sends a disparity cap instead — a bound on the spread between communities rather than on any one community’s level. At N = 30 that difference becomes decisive: Sufficientarian’s absolute cap still yields a verified routing within the one-hour harvest horizon, while all four Equal cells return no verifiable answer at all.

The two objective principles fared better at the top than the caps did. Utilitarian is proven to N = 30 — further up the ladder than any cap-based principle reaches — and is the cheapest condition in the whole study to solve, faster at every size through N = 16 than the baseline that carries no fairness term at all. Its objective prunes the search rather than enlarging it.

What is not settled. Cells above N = 24 were harvested at the one-hour horizon rather than proven, so their values bound what the principle achieves rather than stating it, and they are drawn as isolated points rather than joined to any curve. The attributable differences in Finding 05 rest on N = 22 and 24 only — two fleet sizes.

Method

What counts as a difference

Every claim above uses one test. A difference between two conditions counts only if their means differ by more than the larger of their two permutation bands and the bands do not overlap. The band is measured by re-solving the identical problem under different aircraft orderings, which leaves the feasible set and the optimum untouched and moves only which optimal routing comes back.

Only proven cells contribute to a band. A cell stopped at the harvest horizon sits wherever the search reached, which is not a sample from the optimal set, and averaging it in would widen the band and make every comparison look unattributable. Cells whose phase-2 search produced nothing carry the solver’s unweighted fallback route rather than the principle’s, and are excluded from the tables entirely.

Where this comes from

  • Setup screen and the activity criterion — results/setup_choice.md, harness/activity.py
  • Encoding comparison — results/encoding.jsonl
  • Main ladder, one row per solve — results/fleet_main_metrics.csv; banded cells in the .json
  • Every judgement call, numbered — harness/DECISIONS.md
  • What ran and what broke — harness/NIGHT_REPORT.md
  • The two figures — python figures.py --fleet, plus fig_routes_grid_full() and fig_metric_vs_N_full() for the eight-row and seven-panel variants this page uses
  • Each principle’s own objective, rebuilt from the stored routings so the baseline can be scored on it too — harness/objectives.py, which self-tests against the values the solver reported
  • The figure block and both tables on this page are generated, not typed — harness/findings_page.py rewrites them from the metrics index; --check fails if the page has drifted from it
